name: Autosomal dominant lateral temporal epilepsy
aliases: autosomal dominant partial epilepsy with auditory features

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant focal epilepsy most often caused by variants in LGI1, a secreted neuronal protein that regulates synaptic transmission and excitability in the lateral temporal cortex
The characteristic feature is focal seizures with prominent auditory auras, such as buzzing, ringing or distortion of sounds
Some patients experience receptive aphasic auras, and seizures may be triggered by specific sounds in a subset of families
Onset is typically in adolescence or early adulthood and seizures are usually infrequent and readily controlled
The germline LGI1 variants of this inherited epilepsy are distinct from the acquired anti-LGI1 autoimmune limbic encephalitis, though both implicate the same protein
Brain MRI is usually normal, and interictal EEG may show few or subtle lateral temporal abnormalities
A family history of auditory or aphasic auras is a strong pointer to the diagnosis and should prompt genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Autosomal dominant lateral temporal epilepsy is most commonly caused by loss-of-function variants in LGI1, which encodes leucine-rich glioma-inactivated protein 1, a secreted protein that bridges presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes through interactions with ADAM proteins and helps regulate synaptic excitability and network maturation in the lateral temporal neocortex. Reduced functional LGI1 destabilises excitatory-inhibitory balance in these auditory association regions, generating focal seizures with characteristic auditory or language auras. Notably, the same protein is the target of autoantibodies in an acquired limbic encephalitis, illustrating how genetic and immune disruption of one synaptic protein can each produce epilepsy.
additionalDifferentials: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis
Migraine with auditory or sensory aura
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI, typically normal, to exclude structural temporal lesions
Electroencephalography focusing on the lateral temporal region
Detailed family history documenting auditory or aphasic auras
Autoimmune antibody testing (including anti-LGI1) where an acquired encephalitis is possible
Audiological assessment to exclude a primary auditory cause
redFlags: Subacute cognitive decline, confusion or hyponatraemia suggesting autoimmune LGI1 encephalitis rather than inherited epilepsy
Progressive focal deficit or abnormal MRI indicating a structural lesion
Frequent or drug-resistant seizures requiring reassessment
New behavioural or memory disturbance warranting autoimmune workup
reference.prognosis: Inherited LGI1-related lateral temporal epilepsy is generally benign, with infrequent focal seizures that usually respond well to antiseizure medication and normal cognition between events. This contrasts with the acquired anti-LGI1 encephalitis, which is a more serious condition requiring immunotherapy.
pitfalls: Confusing the benign inherited epilepsy with acquired anti-LGI1 limbic encephalitis, which needs urgent immunotherapy
Dismissing auditory auras as tinnitus or a psychological symptom
Assuming a normal MRI excludes a diagnosis when the condition is typically imaging-negative
Overlooking a familial pattern of auditory or aphasic auras that supports the diagnosis
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
ILAE classification and epilepsy syndrome resources
management: Control focal seizures with antiseizure medication, typically a sodium-channel agent such as carbamazepine or lamotrigine, or levetiracetam
Because seizures are infrequent and usually easily controlled, aim for monotherapy at the lowest effective dose
Give seizure-safety advice and, in families with sound-triggered reflex seizures, counsel avoidance of the identified auditory trigger
Confirm the germline LGI1 diagnosis and actively exclude acquired anti-LGI1 limbic encephalitis, which instead requires immunotherapy
Provide genetic counselling and offer evaluation of relatives, given autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance
Maintain neurology follow-up and reassess the diagnosis if seizures become drug-resistant or cognition deteriorates
